questions.q: What is 'Execute Anonymous,' as described in this lesson?
options: A permanent Apex class that must be deployed before it can run
A tool exclusively for writing Salesforce test coverage reports
A Developer Console window where you paste a block of Apex and run it immediately, without saving it as a permanent class anywhere in the org
A feature that only exists inside VS Code, not the Developer Console
questions.explain: The lesson defines Execute Anonymous as the Developer Console's signature feature for running pasted Apex immediately without saving it permanently -- exactly where you'd paste quick System.debug-laden snippets to check a hypothesis.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does running Execute Anonymous connect directly back to Lesson 12's debugging lesson?
options: Because Execute Anonymous automatically fixes any bugs in the pasted code
Because Lesson 12 required installing VS Code first
Because Execute Anonymous deletes all debug logs automatically
Because it's exactly where you'd paste a snippet full of System.debug statements to see what values are flowing through a piece of logic, without building and deploying a whole class
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties Execute Anonymous to Lesson 12's debugging practice: it's the quick, no-deployment-needed place to run System.debug-laden code and inspect the resulting debug log.

questions.q: What does this lesson say the Salesforce Extensions for VS Code run on top of behind the scenes?
options: The Salesforce CLI -- installing it is a prerequisite even if a developer never types a CLI command directly, since the extensions use it to talk to a Salesforce org
The Developer Console's Execute Anonymous window
A separate browser tab running independently of VS Code
Nothing -- the extensions work entirely standalone with no other tool involved
questions.explain: The lesson states the Salesforce Extensions run on top of the Salesforce CLI, and that installing the CLI is a prerequisite even for developers who never type a CLI command directly.

questions.q: What is a 'scratch org,' per this lesson, and which later course does it say covers this in depth?
options: A permanent production org used only for final deployment, covered in Lesson 16's testing lesson
A disposable, source-driven Salesforce environment created for development and testing, with the full workflow deferred to a dedicated Salesforce DX course later in this path
A type of Apex exception class, covered in Lesson 11
A nickname for the Developer Console itself
questions.explain: The lesson defines a scratch org as a disposable, source-driven environment for development and testing, and explicitly defers the detailed CLI/scratch-org workflow to a dedicated Salesforce DX course later in this path.

questions.q: What is this lesson's overall framing for when to use the Developer Console versus VS Code with the Salesforce Extensions?
options: The Developer Console should always be used instead of VS Code for every task
Both tools are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
VS Code can only be used for non-Salesforce projects
A browser-based tool (Developer Console) for quick, exploratory work, and a full local development environment (VS Code plus Extensions and CLI) for real, version-controlled, team-based development
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the two tools this way: the Developer Console for quick exploratory work, and VS Code with the Extensions and CLI for real, version-controlled, team-based development -- tying back to Lesson 14's version control concepts.
